title: Joseph (Genesis)
description: Biblical figure, son of Jacob and Rachel
wiki_lead:
Joseph (; Hebrew: יוֹסֵף, romanized: Yōsēp̄, lit. 'He shall add') was a dream interpreter and considered an important Hebrew figure in the Bible's Book of Genesis. 
Joseph was the first of the two sons of Jacob and Rachel, making him Jacob's twelfth named child and eleventh son. He is the founder of the Tribe of Joseph among the Israelites. His story functions as an explanation for Israel's residence in Egypt. He is the favourite son of the patriarch Jacob, and his envious brothers sell him into slavery in Biblical Egypt, where he eventually ends up incarcerated. After correctly interpreting the dreams of Pharaoh, he rises to second-in-command in Egypt and saves Egypt during a famine. Jacob's family travels to Egypt to escape the famine, and it is through him that they are given leave to settle in the Land of Goshen (the eastern part of the Nile Delta).
Scholars hold different opinions about the historical background of the Joseph story, as well as the date and development of its composition. Some scholars suggest that the Joseph cycle, i.e. the biblical story of Joseph in Genesis 37-50, was a multigenerational work with both early and late components. Others hold that the original Joseph story was a Persian period diaspora novella told from the perspective of Judeans living in Egypt.
In Jewish tradition, he is the ancestor of a second Messiah called "Mashiach ben Yosef", who will wage war against the forces of evil alongside Mashiach ben David and die in combat with the enemies of God and Israel. Christian tradition often interprets him as a typological precursor to Jesus, emphasizing his virtue and suffering. In Islam, Joseph (Yusuf) is regarded as a prophet, and the Quran recounts his story with some variations, such as the healing of Jacob’s eyes. The Bahá’í faith also references Joseph metaphorically in relation to recognizing manifestations of God. Beyond religious texts, Joseph’s story has inspired extensive literature, music, theater, film and television adaptations.

Etymology
The Bible offers two explanations of the name Yosēf: first, it is compared to the triliteral א־ס־ף (ʾ-s-p), meaning "to gather, remove, take away": "And she conceived, and bore a son; and said, God hath taken away my reproach" (Genesis 30:23); Yosēf is then identified with the similar root יסף (y-s-p), meaning "to add": "And she called his name Joseph; and said, The LORD shall add to me another son." (Genesis 30:24).


Biblical narrative


Birth and family
Joseph, son of Jacob and Rachel, lived in the land of Canaan with ten half brothers, one full brother, and at least one half sister. He was Rachel's firstborn and Jacob's eleventh son. Of all the sons, Joseph was preferred by his father, who gave him a "long coat of many colors". 


Plot against Joseph

Genesis 37, Vayeshev, opens with Joseph and his brothers pasturing Jacob's flock of sheep. He was seventeen years old, and reported critically to Jacob on the actions of his brothers. He then shared with his brothers two dreams he had: in the first dream, Joseph and his brothers gathered bundles of grain, and those gathered by his brothers bowed to his own. In the second dream, the Sun (father), the Moon (mother), and eleven stars (brothers) bowed to Joseph himself. These dreams, implying his supremacy, angered his brothers (Genesis 37:1–11) and made the brothers plot his demise. 

Joseph's half brothers were envious of him. Most of them plotted to kill him in Dothan, except Reuben, who suggested they throw Joseph into an empty cistern; he intended to rescue Joseph himself later. Unaware of this plan to rescue Joseph, the others agreed with Reuben. Upon imprisoning Joseph, the brothers saw a camel caravan carrying spices and perfumes to Egypt, and sold Joseph to these merchants. The guilty brothers painted goat's blood on Joseph's coat and showed it to Jacob, who therefore believed Joseph had died.

grok_lead: Joseph (Genesis) is a central figure in the Hebrew Bible's Book of Genesis, renowned for his narrative of familial betrayal, enslavement, ascension to prominence in Egypt, and ultimate reconciliation with his kin, spanning chapters 37 through 50. Genesis 37-50 As the eleventh son of the patriarch Jacob (also called Israel) and the firstborn of Jacob's favored wife Rachel, Joseph was born after Rachel's long period of infertility, an event marked by her declaration, "May the Lord add to me another son." Genesis 30:22-24 His story exemplifies themes of divine providence, forgiveness, and the preservation of the Israelite lineage amid adversity. scholarly article Joseph's early life was defined by his father's preferential treatment, including the gift of an ornate robeâoften described as a coat of many colorsâwhich symbolized his status as the favored child and fueled resentment from his ten half-brothers. At age seventeen, while tending flocks, Joseph reported unfavorably on his brothers' conduct and shared two prophetic dreams: one of sheaves bowing to his sheaf, and another of celestial bodies prostrating before him, visions that his family interpreted as portents of his future supremacy over them. Enraged, his brothers conspired against him near Dothan, stripping him of his robe, casting him into a dry cistern, and ultimately selling him for twenty shekels of silver to Ishmaelite traders en route to Egypt, deceiving Jacob into believing a wild animal had killed him. In Egypt, Joseph was purchased by Potiphar, captain of Pharaoh's guard, where his administrative acumen and the Lord's blessing led to his promotion as overseer of Potiphar's household. Falsely accused of attempting to assault Potiphar's wife after resisting her advances, Joseph was imprisoned, yet even there he gained favor, managing the other prisoners and interpreting dreams for Pharaoh's chief cupbearer and bakerâforetelling the cupbearer's restoration and the baker's execution. Two years later, the cupbearer recalled Joseph when Pharaoh experienced troubling dreams of seven fat cows devoured by seven gaunt ones and seven healthy ears of grain consumed by seven blighted ones; Joseph interpreted these as harbingers of seven prosperous years followed by seven years of severe famine across the region. Impressed, Pharaoh elevated Joseph to viceroy, second only to himself, tasking him with storing grain during abundance to mitigate the impending crisis; Joseph married Asenath, daughter of an Egyptian priest, and fathered Manasseh and Ephraim. When famine struck Canaan, Joseph's brothers journeyed to Egypt for provisions, unknowingly bowing before him in fulfillment of his youthful dreams; after testing their characterâdemanding Benjamin's presence and staging a theft accusationâJoseph revealed his identity in an emotional reunion, forgiving them and arranging for Jacob and the entire family to settle in Goshen. Jacob's deathbed blessings affirmed Joseph's sons' inheritance within the tribes of Israel, and after Jacob's passing, Joseph reassured his brothers, saying, "You intended to harm me, but God intended it for good to accomplish what is now being done, the saving of many lives" (Genesis 50:20), dying at age 110 and requesting his bones be carried back to Canaan. The Joseph narrative, noted for its literary unity and psychological depth, underscores God's sovereignty in transforming suffering into redemption for the emerging nation of Israel.
